title-group.article-title: Molecular Characteristics of Spontaneous Remission in Major Depressive Disorder: Changes in Serum Acetylcarnitine and Glycerophosphcholine Levels

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Spontaneous remission may influence the outcome of clinical trials and evaluation of antidepressant efficacy, as it is associated with placebo effects and false remission rates. However, the characteristics of spontaneous remission and its biological mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aimed to explore the metabolic signatures and underlying biological mechanisms of spontaneous remission using metabolomics.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This study conducted untargeted and targeted metabolomic analyses in a discovery cohort (n = 16) comprising patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and those who were spontaneously remitted without medication. Findings were validated in an independent cohort (n = 185), comprising drug-treated patients and healthy controls.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Acetylcarnitine levels were significantly increased in spontaneous remission compared to depression, whereas glycerophosphocholine levels were decreased in spontaneous remission. Both metabolites showed the highest concentration in the control group, followed by the remission group, and the lowest concentration in the depression group, regardless of medication status. These changes suggest alterations in mitochondrial and membrane lipid metabolism.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Altered levels in acetylcarnitine and glycerophosphocholine may reflect key pathogenic mechanisms of MDD. These findings offer new insight into spontaneous remission as a distinct clinical subtype of depression and may highlight the potential of these metabolites as biomarkers for treatment monitoring in MDD.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent mental illness characterized by symptoms such as depressed mood, loss of interest, changes in weight or appetite, and suicidal ideation. It is a major cause of disability worldwide [1,2]. Despite the increased prevalence of MDD and the resulting public health burden [3], the proportion of individuals who recognize the condition and seek (and receive) treatment has not improved [4]. Therefore, fundamental improvements, including community-based efforts, are essential to ensure a better diagnosis and treatment of MDD.

MDD has a multifactorial etiology and exhibits clinical heterogeneity among patients. Therefore, its course and prognosis vary widely [5], presenting a challenge for predicting the effectiveness of each treatment and the selection of the most beneficial therapeutic approach [6,7]. Some patients may achieve remission with treatment, while others may exhibit resistance [8,9] or even spontaneous remission without treatment [10]. Spontaneous remission refers to a reduction of depressive symptoms to subclinical levels without therapeutic intervention [10]. It has been reported that 8 to 18% of untreated patients with depression experience spontaneous remission within 12 weeks [11]. A treatment-free trial in outpatients with depression showed that 32% of patients responded positively during follow-up, suggesting that spontaneous remission is common in clinical settings [12]. This phenomenon can contribute to high remission rates in placebo-treated patients in trials evaluating antidepressant efficacy [13], potentially leading to an overestimation of the short-term benefits of certain antidepressants [12]. Despite the reported impact of spontaneous remission on MDD clinical trials and antidepressant evaluations, its nature and mechanisms are unclear, and are often overlooked in research.

Neurobiological evidence from animal models and human spontaneous remission has provided new insights into the underlying mechanisms of depression, spontaneous remission, an potential pharmacological targets [14-16]. MDD is not only associated with changes in brain structure and function, but also in several physiological systems, such as gastrointestinal, immune, endocrine, neural, hormonal, and oxidative stress pathways [17]. Therefore, to characterize and understand the mechanisms of spontaneous remission in depression, it is necessary to explore biomarkers across multiple biological pathways, along with structural and function brain data. Metabolites are small molecules produced during metabolic processes and reflect internal physiological changes across different biochemical pathways influenced by the environment, drugs, nutrition, and stress [18]. The metabolic profile of an individual integrates gene expression and protein activity, and metabolites are indicators of interactions between genetic, proteomic, and environmental factors [19]. Metabolomics, which explore the metabolic dynamics of diseases, might be a useful tool to provide insight into the complex pathophysiology MDD, which involves diverse biologic pathways and the interaction between genetic and environmental factors.

This study aimed to explore the molecular profiles of spontaneous remission that differ from those of depressive states using a metabolomics platform. We examined metabolomic biomarkers associated with the clinical characteristics of spontaneous remission and aimed to identify the molecular mechanisms underlying this phenomenon in depression.

sec.title: Chemicals and Reagents
sec.p: High-performance liquid chromatography-grade methanol, water, and acetonitrile were purchased from J.T. Baker. Formic acid (mass spectrometry grade) was obtained from Fluka Analytical. Four non-endogenous small molecules (sulfamethoxazole, ketoprofen, MES [4-morpholineethanesulfonic acid], and glyphosate) and 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid (HEPES), used for spiking sample for quality control of the analysis, were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. For multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) analysis, standard materials were used to generate calibration curves, and stable isotope-labeled internal standards employed to correct for signal suppression and enhancement [20]. L-acetyl-d3-L-carnitine hydrochloride and glycerophosphocholine standards were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, Acetylcarnitine from Santa Cruz Biotechnology and Sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine-d9 from Toronto Research Chemicals.

sec.title: Sample Collection
sec.p: This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Eulji University (IRB No.: EU24-57). The study was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and all participants signed a written informed consent. The patient group consisted of adult outpatients aged 19 years or older, diagnosed with depression by a board-certified psychiatrist according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)-5 criteria. The severity of depression was assessed using the Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD)-17 items. The remission status was defined as an asymptomatic period of at least 2 months and HAMD score of ≤ 7. The proportion of recurrent MDD patients who experienced two or more depressive episodes was 52.17%. The discovery set included patients with MDD who did not receive medication (ND) and a spontaneous remission group (NR) without medication. The validation set consisted of the ND and NR groups, patients with MDD who received medication (DD), a remission group who received medication (DR), and a healthy control group (Table 1). The DD and DR groups received various types of antidepressants (SSRI, serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor [SNRI], tricyclic antidepressant [TCA], and serotonin modulator) either in monotherapy or in combination. Some patients were also prescribed additional medications, including atypical antipsychotics or non-psychiatric drugs such as probiotics (Bioflor) [21], gastrointestinal agents (Gasmotin) [22], circulatory system drugs (Ginexin-F) [23], antiarrhythmics (Indenol) [24], hormonal therapy (Progynova) [25], antihistamines (Twolion) [26], anti-arteriosclerosis drugs (Vytorin) [27]. This cross-sectional study consisted of a cohort of outpatients with MDD, with no strict control over diet, medication, or lifestyle. The control group consisted of adults with no history of brain trauma, psychiatric medication use, and no alcohol or drug abuse in the prior 6 months. Blood samples were collected in a serum tube without anticoagulants, left at room temperature for 30 minutes to allow coagulation, and then centrifuged at 4,000 × g for 5 minutes. The serum was separated, aliquoted into a 1.5-ml microtubes and stored at −70°C until analysis.

sec.title: Metabolites Extraction and Filtering
sec.p: Thawed serum (100 μl) was transferred into a 1.5-ml tube and mixed with 200 μl of HPLC grade water by a brief vortex. Subsequently, 700 μl of cold 80% methanol was added, vortexed, and samples were stored at −70°C for quenching. Quenched samples were vortexed for 1 minute, sonicated for 10 minutes, incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes, and centrifuged at 14,000 × g and 4°C for 10 minutes. After centrifugation, 400 μl of the supernatant was passed through a nanosep filter using a centrifugation step at 14,000 × g and 4°C for 20 minutes. The filtered sample solution was then transferred to a new 1.5-ml tube. This process was repeated, and the filtered sample was dried using a vacuum concentrator (Scan Vac, LaboGene).

sec.title: Sample Preparation for Untargeted Metabolomics
sec.p: The dried samples were resuspended in 80 μl of HPLC grade water containing 5% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid, and five internal standards (MES, HEPES, and glyphosate at 20 μM concentrations; and ketoprofen and sulfamethoxazole at 10 μM concentrations). Samples were vortexed for 10 minutes, sonicated for 10 minutes, incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes, and centrifuged at 14,000 × g and 4°C for 10 minutes. The supernatant was then diluted 10-fold with the resuspension solution and placed in a mass vial. Analyses were conducted on Agilent 6546 quadrupole time-of-flight (Q-TOF) mass spectrometry system (Agilent Technologies) coupled with Agilent 1290 Infinity II liquid chromatography system. The analytical columns were an Agilent ZORBAX rapid resolution high definition stablebond SB-Aq (2.1 × 150 mm, 1.8 μm) column and an Agilent ZORBAX StableBond-C8 (2.1 × 5 mm, 1.8 μm) guard column, placed in a column oven maintained at 40°C. Mobile phase A consisted of water containing 0.1% formic acid and 5% acetonitrile, and mobile phase B of acetonitrile containing 0.1% formic acid and 5% water. The flow rate of the mobile phase was 400 μl/minutes, and the gradient started at 100% A, decreased to 40% over 14 minutes, then decreased by 35% over 3 minutes, maintained at 5% A for 5 minutes, and then returned to 100% A for the final 5 minutes, for a total of 30 minutes. The Vcap voltage of the ion source capillary was set at 4,000 V and the flow rate of the drying nitrogen gas was 11 L/minutes at 225°C. Data were acquired in the positive ion mode at a scanning speed of 2 Hz.

sec.title: Discovery of Differentially Expressed Metabolites (ND vs. NR)
sec.p: Raw untargeted mass spectrometry data were imported into Profinder (version 10.0, Agilent Technologies) for molecular features (MF) extraction. The CEF file exported from Profinder was then imported into Mass Profiler Professional (version 15.1, Agilent Technologies) for alignment and statistical analysis using a retention time window of 1% + 0.15 minutes and a mass tolerance window of 20 ppm + 0 mDa. Subsequently, MFs commonly detected in all samples of one group were filtered, and volcano plot analysis and partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) were performed. In volcano plot, p values were calculated using the Mann–Whitney unpaired test, and MFs satisfying fold change (FC) > 2 and pvalue<0.05 were listed by comparing the patients with depression and controls. In PLS-DA, variables with variable importance in projection (VIP) > 1 are generally considered relevant to the model [28], and a higher VIP threshold can be applied to select key variables that improve the specificity of the model [29]. This study used VIP > 2 to select key variables for MFs. MS/MS spectra were then acquired for the selected MFs, and compounds identified using Massbank (https://massbank.eu/MassBank/) and the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB, https://hmdb.ca/). Metabolite annotation applied levels 2 and 1, as suggested by the Metabolomics standard initiative [30].

sec.title: Targeted Metabolomics for Metabolite Marker Validation Using Multiple Reaction Monitoring
sec.p: MRM analysis was performed to validate metabolite markers. Thawed serum (100 μl) was transferred into a 1.5-ml tube and mixed with 100 μl of a 5-μg/ml stable isotope-labeled standard solution. The metabolites were extracted and impurities were filtered, as described for non-targeted analysis sample preparation. Analytical standards were diluted in mobile phase A to prepare nine calibration solutions with concentrations of 0, 5, 10, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, and 500 ng/ml. MRM analysis was conducted using an Agilent 6495 triple quadrupole (QQQ) system (Agilent Technologies) coupled with an Agilent 1290 Infinity II liquid chromatography system. The columns and mobile phases were the same as those as those used for non-targeted analysis. The flow rate was 300 μl/minutes, and the mobile phase gradient started at 100% A, decreased to 0% over 5 minutes, and was maintained at 100% A from 7 to 10 minutes. Analysis were performed in the positive ion mode with ion source capillary voltage set to 3,000 V, nozzle voltage to 1,500 V, and sheath gas flow rate at 11 L/minutes at 250°C. The target data peaks obtained through mass spectrometry were quantified using MassHunter Quantitative Analysis (version 10.0; Agilent Technologies).

sec.title: Altered Metabolite Profiles in Untreated Depression and Spontaneous Remission
sec.p: A total of 2,583 MFs were detected in all samples from at least one group. Volcano plot analysis comparing the ND and NR groups identified 130 MFs that met the criteria of FC > 2.0 and p < 0.05. Among these, 92 MFs were upregulated and 38 MFs were downregulated (Fig. 1A). Subsequently, PLS-DA was performed using the 2,538 MF list, yielding a robust distinction model, with an of R2 value of 0.9999 and Q2 value of 0.8654 (Fig. 1B, 1C). A total of 228 MFs were listed by integrating 130 MFs identified from volcano plot analysis and 170 MFs showing VIP > 2 from PLS-DA (Supplementary Table 1; available online). MS/MS spectra were acquired for these 228 MFs.

Metabolite identification followed the Metabolomics Standard Initiative criteria. For level 2 identification, MS/MS spectra were first matched to experimental data, using Massbank and HMDB. Level 1 identification was confirmed by analyzing standard compounds under identical conditions. Acetylcarnitine and glycerophosphocholine were validated and selected as final markers (Table 2). Acetylcarnitine was significantly increased in the NR group compared with ND (p = 0.003, FC = 2.74), while glycerophosphocholine was reduced (p = 0.001, FC = 2.72) (Fig. 2).

sec.title: Quantitative Validation of Altered Metabolite Markers in Spontaneous Remission
sec.p: To validate these findings, we examined a larger sample pool and assessed comparisons according to drug treatment. The validation set included DD, DR, and healthy controls, in addition to ND and NR. Compound optimization was performed using standard solutions of acetylcarnitine, glycerophosphocholine, and isotope-labeled standard solutions to optimize the MRM transitions of the analytes (Supplementary Table 2; available online).

Similar to the untargeted analysis conducted at the marker discovery stage, the NR group showed an increase in acetylcarnitine and decrease in glycerophosphocholine levels (Fig. 3A, 3D). In the DR group (remission state receiving drug treatment), acetylcarnitine levels were also increased (Fig. 3B), whereas glycerophosphocholine showed the opposite trend, varying with drug treatment (Fig. 3E). Regardless of drug treatment, acetylcarnitine and glycerophosphocholine showed the highest concentrations in the healthy control group, followed by the remission state, and the lowest concentrations in the depressed state (Fig. 3C, 3F). Glycerophosphocholine showed significant differences in all group comparisons (depression, remission, and healthy) (Fig. 3F).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This study identified two serum metabolites significantly altered between untreated depression and spontaneous remission. These findings were validated in a large sample pool including healthy controls and individuals receiving medication. Acetylcarnitine consistently increased in remission regardless of medication, while glycerophosphocholine showed the opposite trend depending on medication intervention. Both metabolites increased from depression to remission to healthy controls, with demonstrating differences in all comparisons. These findings may provide new insights into the molecular characteristics and response to therapy of spontaneous remission, one of the clinical subtypes of depression.

Acetylcarnitine, an acetylated derivative of carnitine, is an endogenous compound found in several tissues, including the brain [31]. De novo acetylcarnitine synthesis is catalyzed by carnitine acetyltransferase (CAT), located in the inner mitochondrial membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, and peroxide vesicles. CAT catalyzes the transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) to carnitine to produce acetylcarnitine and free CoA [32]. The synthesized acetylcarnitine is then transported to the cytosol by the enzyme carnitine/acetylcarnitine translocase (CACT), where it plays a role in the beta-oxidation of fatty acids [33]. Acetylcarnitine promotes the uptake of acetyl-CoA into mitochondria during fatty acid oxidation, enhancing acetylcholine production, stimulating protein and membrane phospholipid synthesis, and preventing excessive neuronal cell death [34]. Previous studies have reported altered acetylcarnitine levels and abnormalities in lipid metabolism in depressive states, potentially resulting in impaired neuroplasticity, a key pathogenic mechanisms of MDD [34]. Furthermore, previous studies have reported decreased acetylcarnitine levels in patients with MDD compared with healthy controls, with normalization in those achieving remission [35,36]. Our findings align with these results, with the decrease in peripheral acetylcarnitine levels in a depressed state being suggestive of impaired mitochondrial metabolism of carnitine to acetylcarnitine, which may ultimately compromise lipid metabolism and mitochondrial energy metabolism in MDD.

As a direct result of intracellular calcium influx and calcium overload, calcium-dependent phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) is activated, and phospholipids, such as phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, which are major components of cell membranes, are degraded [37]. Phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine are deacylated to lysophosphatidylcholine and lysophosphatidylethanolamine, respectively, which are then converted to glycerophosphocholine and glycerophosphoethanolamine, respectively, by lysophospholipase [37,38]. A previous study in patients with depression reported that these compounds resulting from membrane phospholipid degradation were increased in the white matter in late-life depression, suggesting that this could result in altered phospholipid metabolism, inflammation, and neurodegeneration [38]. A recent study that integrated functional connectivity (FC) and plasma lipid metabolite profiling of the brains of patients with depression showed that glycerophosphocholine levels were negatively correlated with FC in the right middle frontal gyrus, right anterior cingulate gyrus, and pericingual gyrus, suggesting that changes in FC in patients with MDD are related to synaptic plasticity and serotonin dysregulation [39]. Furthermore, others have reported increased blood glycerophosphocholesterol levels in patients with depression compared to those in controls [40,41], with a reestablishment following treatment with antidepressants [40]. Consistent with these findings, we showed that glycerophosphocholine levels increased in untreated depression compared with that in the spontaneous remission state. Integrated analysis of the gut microbiota profile and blood metabolites suggested that the oxidation of glycerophosphocholine may contribute to the pathogenesis of MDD, through the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome pathway and lipid metabolism [42]. Therefore, the observed changes in glycerophosphocholine levels may provide a link to the inflammatory and lipid metabolism abnormalities observed in MDD.

Additionally, animal studies suggest that acetylcarnitine administration alters the composition of the mitochondrial inner membrane proteins in the cerebellum and affects the levels of glycerophosphocholine, potentially through the interaction with cytoskeletal proteins and alteration of membrane dynamics in the vicinity of the glycerol backbone of the phospholipid bilayer, contributing to membrane stability [33]. Together, these two metabolites may reflect changes in membrane lipid metabolism and mitochondrial energy metabolism, associated may with the pathophysiological mechanisms of depression. Both acetylcarnitine and glycerophosphocholine can cross the blood-brain barrier, supporting their relevance as peripheral biomarkers of central changes in MDD. The administration of these metabolites in animals promoted antidepressant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects [43,44], suggesting that changes in the endogenous levels of these metabolites might be related to pathogenic mechanisms of depression, and be indicative of therapeutic responses, highlighting their potential as biomarkers for MDD.

This study shows some limitations. First, the main treatment strategy for MDD is antidepressants, as such, it is difficult to recruit patients that show spontaneous remission without drug treatment. Therefore, the sample size of the spontaneous remission group was relatively small compared with that of the other groups, which may limit statistical power. Validation in a large sample group that considers appropriate effect size and power is necessary to strengthen our findings. Among all MDD patients, the proportion of recurrent patients with 2 or more depressive episodes was 52.17%. Previous studies have reported changes in the proteomic profile in relapse [45], and this heterogeneity of depressive states may also affect the metabolomic profiles. Although sex and body mass index were matched between groups, age differences in some groups within the validation may have introduced variability (Supplementary Table 3; available online). In addition, a subset of MDD patients presented comorbidities (assessed through a questionnaire), including diabetes (15.35%), hypertension (27.83%), hyperlipidemia (20.87%), and gastrointestinal diseases (7.83%). These diseases involve metabolic changes, which can represent confounding variables. This study is a preliminary study based on a cohort of outpatient MDD patients, and rigorous control over lifestyle, medication, and comorbidities was not feasible. Future research should include subgroup analyses to account for these variables, which will allow a more refined exploration of metabolic dynamics related to MDD. Furthermore, although volcano plot analysis was used in the discovery phase, multiple testing correction was not applied. Considering the large number of metabolites examined, it is necessary to control the influence of type 1 error through multiple testing. In addition, quantitative changes in the overall associated metabolic processes were not identified. Future work should explore network-level alterations and underlying mechanism to establish comprehensive metabolic key signatures and pathways in MDD. These analyses would enable the identification of reliable biomarkers and novel therapeutic targets.

In conclusion, we identified altered metabolic profiles in spontaneous remission compared with those in untreated depression. The changes in acetylcarnitine and glycerophosphocholine may be related to the pathophysiology of MDD, reflecting dysregulated lipid metabolism related to mitochondria and cell membranes. These findings provide new information regarding spontaneous remission, a subtype of depression whose molecular mechanisms are poorly understood, and present promising biomarkers for the subtyping and treatment of MDD.
